my_sentence: Today I recited some English words and listen to some English podcasts.
correction: Today I recited some English words and listened to some English podcasts.
explanation: The two completed activities need parallel past-tense verbs: "recited" and "listened." The teacher prompted the past form.
correct_examples: I read a book and listened to music yesterday.
She studied vocabulary and watched a lecture.
context: Describing what he did that day.

my_sentence: I had a good time to listen to them.
correction: I had a good time listening to them.
explanation: After "have a good time," use a gerund: "have a good time doing something," not an infinitive.
correct_examples: We had a good time visiting the museum.
She had a good time talking with her friends.
context: Talking about listening to English podcasts.

my_sentence: There are only a few rich people and a lot of poor.
correction: There are only a few rich people and a lot of poor ones.
explanation: When "the poor" is not used as a fixed group noun, add a noun or substitute such as "poor ones" after "a lot of."
correct_examples: A few rich people and many poor ones live in the city.
Some people are wealthy, while others are poor.
context: Explaining an unequal market.

my_sentence: The rich already have big houses and enough resources.
correction: The rich can already have big houses and enough resources.
explanation: The teacher was expressing a possible situation, so the modal "can" was needed before the base verb "have."
correct_examples: A large company can already have enough staff.
Some families can already afford a second home.
context: Describing the possible advantages of wealthy people.

my_sentence: Because of there's don't have enough consumers.
correction: Because they don't have enough consumers.
explanation: Use the subject pronoun "they" before the verb. "There's" means "there is" and cannot refer to the poor people here.
correct_examples: They cannot expand because they do not have enough customers.
They are struggling because they lack consumers.
context: Explaining why a stagnant market lacks buyers.

my_sentence: The market can be stop.
correction: The market can be stopped.
explanation: After the modal "can" and passive auxiliary "be," use the past participle "stopped."
correct_examples: The service can be stopped at any time.
A market can be affected by weak demand.
context: Explaining what stagnation means.

my_sentence: They can't run out of they are money.
correction: They don't have any money to use.
explanation: The intended meaning is lack of money. Use the possessive adjective "their" correctly, and say "don't have any money to use" rather than "run out of they are money."
correct_examples: They don't have any money to use.
Poor families may not have enough money for food.
context: Explaining why poor people cannot keep spending.

my_sentence: If they don't have enough consumer, their company will go bankrupt.
correction: If they don't have enough consumers, their company will go bankrupt.
explanation: After the plural quantifier "enough" in this context, use the plural count noun "consumers."
correct_examples: The store needs enough consumers to survive.
Without enough customers, the business may close.
context: Explaining why rich companies still need buyers.

my_sentence: The economic will be pretty good.
correction: The economy will be pretty good.
explanation: "Economy" is the noun for a country's financial system; "economic" is an adjective.
correct_examples: The economy is growing quickly.
A strong economy can create jobs.
context: Predicting the result of a mostly middle-class society.

my_sentence: Which situation can arrive more?
correction: Which situation can thrive more?
explanation: The intended meaning is "develop successfully," so the verb is "thrive," not "arrive."
correct_examples: Small businesses can thrive in a healthy economy.
The community began to thrive after new jobs appeared.
context: Comparing two economic situations.

my_sentence: We expect our market to become more and more better.
correction: We expect our market to become much better.
explanation: Do not combine "more and more" with the comparative "better." Use "much better" or "better and better."
correct_examples: We expect the service to become much better.
The situation is getting better and better.
context: Explaining why a stagnant market is a disadvantage.

my_sentence: Their economic is keeping the same level for many years.
correction: Their economy is keeping the same level for many years.
explanation: The subject is a financial system, so use the noun "economy," not the adjective "economic."
correct_examples: Their economy has stayed at the same level for years.
The economy is recovering slowly.
context: Describing Japan's long-term economic performance.

my_sentence: A decade years ago, their salary was higher.
correction: A decade ago, their salary was higher.
explanation: "A decade" already means ten years, so do not add the plural noun "years" after it.
correct_examples: A decade ago, I lived in Tokyo.
The company was smaller a decade ago.
context: Comparing salaries ten years ago with current salaries.

my_sentence: Their currency is a continuing drop.
correction: Their currency is continuing to drop.
explanation: After "is continuing," use the infinitive "to drop" to describe an ongoing change.
correct_examples: Prices are continuing to rise.
The exchange rate is continuing to change.
context: Discussing the falling value of the yen.

my_sentence: In some industry, they were defeated by China.
correction: In some industries, they were defeated by China.
explanation: The phrase refers to more than one area of business, so use the plural noun "industries."
correct_examples: China is competitive in some industries.
Several industries were affected by the policy.
context: Comparing Japanese and Chinese industries.

my_sentence: Japan lost their position.
correction: The country lost its position.
explanation: A country is singular, so use the singular possessive pronoun "its," not "their." The teacher also recast "Japan" as "the country."
correct_examples: The country lost its position in the market.
The company lost its advantage.
context: Discussing Japan's reduced position in car exports.

my_sentence: I don't think it's our responsibilities.
correction: I don't think it's our responsibility.
explanation: Here "responsibility" refers to one general duty, so use the singular uncountable form.
correct_examples: It is not our responsibility to solve every problem.
Helping is a personal responsibility.
context: Discussing whether people must help others.

my_sentence: It is your responsibility to help them.
correction: It is your responsibility to help him or her.
explanation: The teacher was referring to one specific person, so the singular object pronouns are "him or her" rather than the plural "them."
correct_examples: It is not your responsibility to support him or her.
She asked me to help her.
context: Discussing responsibility for a stranger's choices.

my_sentence: They made a significant difference.
correction: They can make a significant difference.
explanation: The sentence describes a possible effect, so use the modal "can" and the base verb "make."
correct_examples: A small donation can make a significant difference.
Good training can make a difference.
context: Explaining what wealthy people can do for society.

my_sentence: They can donate hundred thousand or one million.
correction: They can donate hundreds of thousands or one million.
explanation: Use "hundreds of thousands" when the exact number is not specified; the plural form needs "of" before the following noun.
correct_examples: The company donated hundreds of thousands of dollars.
They raised hundreds of thousands for the project.
context: Discussing celebrity donations.

my_sentence: It is little for their fortune.
correction: It is little compared to their fortune.
explanation: Use "little compared to" to compare a donation with a person's total wealth.
correct_examples: The cost is little compared to his income.
The donation was small compared to the company's fortune.
context: Evaluating a donation relative to a celebrity's wealth.

my_sentence: Their salary are not enough.
correction: Their salary is not enough.
explanation: The subject "salary" is singular, so use "is." Use "salaries are" only when referring to multiple salaries.
correct_examples: His salary is not enough to support his family.
Their salaries are different.
context: Explaining why poor people should not pay the same taxes.

my_sentence: You can't expect them pay the same taxes.
correction: You can't expect them to pay the same taxes.
explanation: The pattern is "expect someone to do something," so the infinitive marker "to" is required after "them."
correct_examples: You cannot expect them to pay the same amount.
We expect employees to follow the rules.
context: Comparing tax burdens for rich and poor people.

my_sentence: When they buy some product in the supermarket.
correction: When they buy some products in the supermarket.
explanation: With "some" and a count noun in this general example, use the plural "products."
correct_examples: People compare products before buying them.
They bought some products at the supermarket.
context: Making an example about ethical shopping.

my_sentence: You need to demonstrator the result.
correction: You need to demonstrate the result.
explanation: "Demonstrate" is the verb needed after "need to." "Demonstrator" is a person or device, not the action.
correct_examples: You need to demonstrate the result clearly.
The experiment demonstrates the effect.
context: Explaining the difference between a conclusion and supporting evidence.

my_sentence: Tell us what should we do.
correction: Tell us what we should do.
explanation: An embedded question uses statement word order: subject before the modal, as in "what we should do."
correct_examples: Please tell me what we should do next.
She explained what we should prepare.
context: Explaining what a conclusion should tell people.

my_sentence: You can donate your money to a charity.
correction: You can donate your money to charity.
explanation: When speaking about charitable activity in general, "charity" is normally uncountable and takes no article.
correct_examples: Many people donate to charity.
She gives money to charity every year.
context: Using the word "charity" in a sentence.

my_sentence: We need to contribute our experience and skills to make our society become better.
correction: We need to contribute to society to make it better.
explanation: The natural collocation is "contribute to society." Once "society" is the object, use the pronoun "it" in the second clause.
correct_examples: Volunteers contribute to society by helping others.
Education can make society better.
context: Explaining how people can improve society.

my_sentence: Some people are less fortune than me.
correction: Some people are less fortunate than me.
explanation: After "are less," use the adjective "fortunate." "Fortune" is a noun.
correct_examples: Many people are less fortunate than us.
He was fortunate to find a job.
context: Talking about people with fewer advantages.

my_sentence: He wants to get a prominent position from his company.
correction: He wants to have a prominent position in his company.
explanation: The natural collocation is "have a position in a company." Use "in" for the organization where the position exists.
correct_examples: She has a prominent position in the company.
He wants to have a senior position in finance.
context: Practising the word "prominent."

my_sentence: You shouldn't be obligated to ask your children do something they don't like.
correction: You shouldn't be obligated to ask your children to do something they don't like.
explanation: The pattern is "ask someone to do something," so add "to" before the base verb after "your children."
correct_examples: You should not ask children to do things they hate.
They asked me to wait outside.
context: Discussing parental obligations and choices.

my_sentence: The schemer needed to use social engineering to cheat others.
correction: The schemer needed to use social engineering to cheat on others.
explanation: In the teacher's model, the phrase was "cheat on others." Keep the preposition when using this collocation.
correct_examples: He tried to cheat on other people.
The scammer cheated on his customers.
context: Creating an example with "social engineering."

my_sentence: We need to define some basic rule to limit our behavior.
correction: We need to define some basic rules to limit our behavior.
explanation: The quantifier "some" requires the plural count noun "rules."
correct_examples: We need to define some basic rules.
The school has strict rules about safety.
context: Using the word "define."

my_sentence: They tried to eradicate this danger to protect more people.
correction: They tried to eradicate the disease to protect more people.
explanation: "Eradicate" means completely remove something harmful. In this example, the intended object was "the disease," not the general noun "danger."
correct_examples: Scientists hope to eradicate the disease.
The campaign aims to eradicate corruption.
context: Creating a sentence with "eradicate."

my_sentence: A group of people want to build a utopia for their children.
correction: A group of people wants to build a utopia for their children.
explanation: The head noun is the singular "group," so the present-tense verb is "wants."
correct_examples: A group of students wants to visit the museum.
A team of engineers wants to improve the design.
context: Creating a sentence with "utopia."

my_sentence: It can help our society more stable.
correction: It can help our society become more stable.
explanation: After "help someone," use a base verb such as "become" before an adjective describing a change.
correct_examples: The policy can help the economy become more stable.
Exercise helps people become healthier.
context: Explaining a possible benefit of social support.

my_sentence: This kind of cases can be reduced.
correction: These kinds of cases can be reduced.
explanation: Because "cases" is plural, use the plural demonstrative and noun: "these kinds of cases."
correct_examples: These kinds of cases are difficult to solve.
We should prevent these kinds of problems.
context: Describing different criminal cases.

my_sentence: They can use their abilities to make their own money.
correction: They can use their skills to earn their own money.
explanation: The teacher preferred the more specific noun "skills" and the natural collocation "earn money," rather than "make money" in this sentence.
correct_examples: People can use their skills to earn money.
She earns her own money through freelance work.
context: Discussing jobs that can help people escape poverty.

my_sentence: Give people some hopes.
correction: Give people some hope.
explanation: "Hope" is uncountable when it means a feeling or positive expectation, so do not pluralize it here.
correct_examples: The message gave people some hope.
Her support gave me hope.
context: Listing the benefits of helping poor people.

my_sentence: To give our sense of security.
correction: To give us a sense of security.
explanation: After "give," use the object pronoun "us," not the possessive determiner "our." The noun phrase also needs the article "a."
correct_examples: This policy gives us a sense of security.
The job gave her a sense of purpose.
context: Explaining how social support can make people feel safer.

my_sentence: That can support you overcome these problems.
correction: That can support you to overcome these problems.
explanation: In the teacher's version, "support someone to do something" was used, so include "to" before the infinitive.
correct_examples: The program supports people to overcome difficulties.
Her family supported her to finish school.
context: Explaining how insurance can help someone recover.

my_sentence: Almost my students were poor.
correction: Almost all of the students were poor.
explanation: Before a plural noun phrase, use "almost all of the students," not "almost students."
correct_examples: Almost all of the students passed.
Almost all of my friends live nearby.
context: Recalling his students when he had little money.

my_sentence: They had too many hope.
correction: They had too much hope.
explanation: When "hope" means a general feeling, it is uncountable, so use "much" rather than "many."
correct_examples: They still have too much hope in that plan.
A little hope can keep people going.
context: Discussing people who hoped for a better future.

my_sentence: During my childhood, most of parents expected their children could go to college.
correction: During my childhood, most of the parents expected their children to go to college.
explanation: Use "most of the parents" for a specific group, and use the pattern "expect someone to do something."
correct_examples: Most of the parents expected their children to attend college.
We expected him to arrive early.
context: Explaining parents' hopes for their children.

my_sentence: Most of them can't finish their dream.
correction: Most of them couldn't finish their dreams.
explanation: The story is in the past, so use "couldn't." The plural subject "most of them" also refers to multiple "dreams."
correct_examples: Many students could not finish their studies.
They couldn't achieve their dreams at that time.
context: Describing childhood expectations that were not fulfilled.

my_sentence: At the end, they didn't enter college.
correction: In the end, they didn't enter college.
explanation: Use the fixed linking phrase "in the end" to mean finally or after everything happened.
correct_examples: In the end, she decided to stay.
In the end, they found a solution.
context: Concluding the story about the parents' hopes.

my_sentence: It can help you more focus on your tasks.
correction: It can help you focus on your tasks.
explanation: After "help someone," use the base verb directly: "help you focus." Do not insert "more" before the verb here.
correct_examples: A clear plan can help you focus on your work.
Music helps me concentrate.
context: Explaining how hope can motivate people.

my_sentence: If you can't find any hope, you can't insistent.
correction: If you can't find any hope, you can't insist.
explanation: After the modal "can't," use the base-form verb "insist," not the adjective-like form "insistent."
correct_examples: If you lose hope, you may not insist on trying.
She insisted on finishing the work.
context: Explaining why people may give up.

my_sentence: Hope is like an energy to push your go ahead.
correction: Hope is like an energy to push you to go ahead.
explanation: The pattern is "push someone to do something." Use the object pronoun "you" and add "to" before the verb.
correct_examples: Her support pushed me to go ahead.
The goal pushed him to work harder.
context: Explaining how hope motivates people.

my_sentence: They can came back to the society.
correction: They can come back to society.
explanation: After the modal "can," use the base form "come." The general noun "society" normally takes no article here.
correct_examples: Training can help people come back to society.
She came back to society after receiving support.
context: Discussing education and opportunities for poor people.

my_sentence: When the shopping online was not popular.
correction: When shopping online was not popular.
explanation: The activity "shopping online" is used as a gerund phrase here, so it does not need the article "the."
correct_examples: When online shopping was new, people were cautious.
Online shopping became popular quickly.
context: Explaining why a transaction platform was created.

my_sentence: The company find a problem and they build a platform.
correction: The company found a problem and they built a platform.
explanation: The events happened in the past, so use the simple past forms "found" and "built."
correct_examples: They found a problem and built a new system.
The team discovered the issue and fixed it.
context: Describing how Taobao addressed the trust problem.

my_sentence: The problem can be finished.
correction: The problem can be fixed.
explanation: For solving a problem, use the collocation "fix a problem." "Finish" is normally used for an activity or task.
correct_examples: The platform can fix the problem.
The engineers fixed the issue quickly.
context: Explaining the role of the online platform.

my_sentence: If there are too many these kind of cases, students can't trust the teacher.
correction: If there are too many kinds of these cases, students can't trust the teacher.
explanation: After "too many," use the plural noun "kinds." The teacher recast the phrase as "too many kinds of these cases."
correct_examples: Too many kinds of scams can reduce trust.
There are several kinds of online fraud.
context: Discussing repeated scams involving private classes.

my_sentence: If he want to get the money back, he needed to pay more.
correction: If he wanted to get the money back, he needed to pay more.
explanation: The hypothetical condition uses the past form "wanted" after "if" to match the teacher's second-conditional-style sentence.
correct_examples: If he wanted a refund, he needed to file a claim.
If she wanted to leave, she had to explain why.
context: Discussing the cost of trying to recover stolen money.

my_sentence: He needed to go Philippine to find the money.
correction: He needed to go to the Philippines to find the money.
explanation: Use the preposition "to" before a destination, and use the country name "the Philippines."
correct_examples: She went to the Philippines for work.
He needed to go to Manila.
context: Discussing whether the victim should travel to recover the money.

my_sentence: He could borrow a lot of money to a teacher.
correction: He could lend a lot of money to a teacher.
explanation: The person giving money lends it; the person receiving it borrows it. Here the victim would give money to the teacher, so use "lend."
correct_examples: He lent money to a friend.
She borrowed money from the bank.
context: Describing the victim's financial situation.

my_sentence: It is not belong to everyone.
correction: It does not belong to everyone.
explanation: The verb "belong" is an ordinary present-tense verb, so make the negative with "does not," not "is not."
correct_examples: This benefit does not belong to everyone.
The responsibility does not belong to him.
context: Explaining who qualifies for government-paid medical bills.

my_sentence: It's only for some very poor people.
correction: It's only to some very poor people.
explanation: The teacher used "to some people" when describing who receives the benefit. Use the recipient preposition "to" in that structure.
correct_examples: The program is available to some poor families.
The money was given to people in need.
context: Clarifying the limited recipients of a benefit.

my_sentence: The government want to reduce its influence.
correction: The government wants to reduce its influence.
explanation: The singular subject "government" takes the third-person singular verb "wants."
correct_examples: The government wants to reduce costs.
The company wants to improve its service.
context: Explaining why the government may pay certain medical bills.

my_sentence: There are too many factors will affect the money.
correction: There are too many factors that will affect the money.
explanation: A full clause after "factors" needs a relative pronoun such as "that": "factors that will affect..."
correct_examples: Many factors can affect the final price.
There are several factors that will affect the result.
context: Explaining why reimbursement varies between hospitals.

my_sentence: They don't have choice.
correction: They didn't have any choices.
explanation: For the past situation, use "didn't have." The teacher also used the plural count noun phrase "any choices."
correct_examples: They didn't have any choices at the time.
When money is tight, people may feel they have no choice.
context: Explaining why people accept tiring jobs.
